subject: operating-systems
title: Directories and naming
summary: Directories map names to file-system objects and provide the namespace used for path resolution.

questions.prompt: What is the main role of a directory?
options: Map names to file objects or identifiers
questions.answerKey: A directory provides name-to-object mappings in the file-system namespace.
questions.explanation: Directory data may itself be stored as a file-system object.

questions.prompt: What does an absolute path normally begin from?
options: The file-system root or another global namespace root
questions.answerKey: An absolute path is resolved from the namespace root rather than the caller current directory.
questions.explanation: The syntax for roots varies across systems.

questions.prompt: A process changes its current directory to /var/log and opens notes.txt with a relative path. Which object is used to resolve the name?
questions.answerKey: Relative paths are resolved from the process current working directory.
questions.explanation: An explicit directory handle can also be used by APIs that support it.

questions.prompt: Why can hard links be restricted for directories?
options: Unrestricted directory links could create namespace cycles and complicate traversal
questions.answerKey: Directory cycles would complicate tree assumptions, deletion, and traversal algorithms.
questions.explanation: File-system implementations may support controlled directory links such as symbolic links.

questions.prompt: Compare a hard link and a symbolic link.
questions.answerKey: A hard link is another directory name for the same underlying file object, so it usually shares inode/object identity and data. A symbolic link is a separate object containing a path to resolve, which can dangle when the target name disappears.
questions.explanation: Terminology differs, but the identity-versus-path distinction is central.

questions.prompt: Describe the major steps in resolving /a/b/c from the root.
questions.answerKey: Start at the root, look up a in the root directory, verify traversal permissions and obtain its directory object, then look up b and repeat; finally resolve c and check the requested operation permissions and object type.
questions.explanation: Path resolution may also follow mount points or symbolic links, depending on policy.
